title: Harnessing resonant dipolar interactions in a hybrid atom-molecule quantum system
authors: Daniel K. Ruttley, Tom R. Hepworth, Juan M. García-Garrido, Caleb J. H. Rich, Rosario González-Férez, Alexander Guttridge, Simon L. Cornish
abstract: Hybrid quantum systems offer a route to combining the complementary strengths of distinct quantum platforms while mitigating their limitations. A particularly promising architecture combines neutral atoms and polar molecules: atoms provide fast, controllable interactions through excitation to Rydberg states, while molecules possess long-lived rotational states that are attractive for quantum memories and qudits. Although dipolar interactions between atoms and molecules have been observed in gas-phase and beam experiments, they have not previously been explored in a scalable optical tweezer platform that enables the controlled coherent interactions needed for quantum state transfer and entanglement. Here, we realise this goal, demonstrating coherent dipolar interactions between an individual Rydberg atom and an individual polar molecule. The separation of the particles is controlled using species-specific optical tweezers and their dipolar interactions are made strongly state-dependent by tuning two atom-molecule pair states into resonance. We exploit these interactions to demonstrate atom-mediated state readout of a molecular qubit, observe coherent spin exchange between the particles, and generate entanglement using a blockade-based controlled-NOT operation. Together, these results establish a coherent atom-molecule interface in which long-lived molecular quantum information can be rapidly mapped onto internal states of a Rydberg atom for readout or onward coherent transfer. This platform can be scaled to realise hybrid quantum processors utilising atom-mediated readout and entanglement of molecular qubits and mixed-species quantum simulators of dipolar systems.
summary: The researchers demonstrated coherent dipole-dipole coupling between Rydberg atoms and polar molecules trapped in optical tweezers. By exploiting resonance, they achieved strong, controlled interactions necessary for quantum information processing tasks. This establishes a scalable hybrid platform capable of mapping molecular quantum information onto atomic states.
main_problem: The primary goal was to realize controlled, coherent dipolar interactions between an individual Rydberg atom and an individual polar molecule within a scalable optical tweezer platform.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated these coherent dipolar interactions, enabling molecular state readout, observation of spin exchange, and the generation of entanglement via a blockade-based CNOT operation.
method: They used species-specific optical tweezers to trap atoms (e.g., Rb) and molecules (e.g., RbCs), tuning atomic and molecular states into resonance to engineer strong dipole-dipole coupling.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid quantum platform combining neutral Rydberg atoms and polar molecules, governed by an engineered dipole-dipole interaction Hamiltonian ($H_{dd} \propto 1/R^3$). The interactions are controlled by tuning the energy levels into resonance using external fields.
key_observables: Coherent dipolar coupling strength ($	ext{MHz}$-scale), blockade signatures (suppression of atomic excitation), molecular state readout fidelity, and entanglement fidelity ($F$).
important_parameters: Resonance condition achieved by matching transition energies; interaction strengths scale as $1/R^3$ at resonance; measurement fidelities reached $\approx 0.91$.
main_assumptions: The dipolar description is accurate for separations $R \gtrsim 1 \mu	ext{m}$; the analysis relies on postselection to filter out certain error channels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup, energy level diagrams showing resonant pairs, and experimental results demonstrating blockade dependence on distance and molecular state, as well as Rabi oscillations used for readout.
paper_structure: The work progresses from establishing the feasibility of controlled dipolar interactions in optical tweezers to demonstrating specific quantum operations: first, molecular-state readout via Rydberg blockade; second, observing coherent spin exchange dynamics; and finally, generating entanglement using a CNOT gate.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant step toward building hybrid quantum processors by establishing a robust, controllable interface between two distinct quantum matter systems (atoms and molecules) using long-range dipolar interactions.
